list.listitem: Chronic pelvic pain is common in women of all age groups and can lead to disability and distress resulting in significant personal and healthcare costs. C
No single test or group of tests is recommended, and laboratory, radiologic, or surgical diagnostic interventions should be guided by the history and physical examination. C
The pathophysiology of chronic pelvic pain is not well understood; its treatment is often unsatisfactory and limited to symptom relief. C

The main approaches to treatment are multidisciplinary and include counseling, analgesics, horomone therapy, B manual therapy, surgery to interrupt nerve pathways, B and providing reassurance using laparoscopy to exclude serious pathology. C

background.definition: Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is defined as non-menstrual pain lasting for >6 months that is severe to the point of causing functional disability or requiring medical / surgical treatment. CPP has no single identifiable cause and is conceptualized as a chronic regional pain syndrome or functional somatic pain syndrome.

list.listitem: It is estimated that between 4% to 20% of women between the ages of 15 and 50 years suffer from chronic pelvic pain at some point in their lives, but the true incidence, prevalence, and socioeconomic impact of CPP remains unknown..

A 1996 survey estimated the direct health care costs at 880 million dollars, with out-of-pocket expenses of nearly 2 billion dollars. Indirect costs, such as loss of work, were estimated at greater than 500 million dollars.
Another survey in 2019 revealed that CPP has a cost of $16,970 to $20,898 per woman per year due to productivity loss. There was a significant direct association between pain scores and overall cost.

CPP accounts for approximately 1 in 10 outpatient gynecologic visits for women, 15% to 40% of listed indications for diagnostic laparoscopy, and 10% to 20% of listed indications for hysterectomy in the U.S. and Canada.

In a study of 424 participants with urological CPP syndromes, over one third (38%) had a non-urological-associated somatic syndrome including irritable bowel syndrome (22%), fibromyalgia (4%), chronic fatigue syndrome (3%) or multiple syndromes (10%). Patients with these comorbid conditions reported more severe urological symptoms and more frequent depression and anxiety.
The causes of CPP are diverse with etiologies including gynecologic, urologic, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, and psychoneurologic.

Four conditions account for majority of the cases of CPP: endometriosis, adhesions, interstitial cystitis, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). More than one source of pain can be found in the same patient.
There is some evidence of genetic risk factors for pelvic pain of urologic origin.
Pelvic venous insufficiency (retrograde flow in the gonadal and internal iliac veins) is believed to be the underlying cause of pelvic congestion syndrome leading to CPP.

In women with CPP, multiple factors are likely involved. Inflammation from infection or endometriosis can lead to prolonged pain. Persistent pain can increase excitability of neurons within the spinal cord leading to an increase in pain perception in visceral organs.

It is not clear how lesions in women with endometriosis correlate to the level of pain experienced. In one study of 96 women with pelvic pain from endometriosis, dysuria and midline anterior pain were the only symptoms associated with location of a superficial endometriosis lesion. Of these women, only a few had deeply infiltrating lesions.33

Current evidence points to excessive production and release of endometrial prostaglandins (PGs) during menstruation in women with dysmenorrhea, causing abnormal uterine hypercontractility, reduced uterine blood flow, uterine hypoxia, and hypersensitization of pain fibers by PGs.

list.listitem: CPP has an extremely broad differential diagnosis including gynecologic, gastrointestinal, urinary, neurologic, musculoskeletal, and psychologic disorders. C
No single test or group of tests is recommended, and laboratory, radiologic, or surgical diagnostic interventions should be guided by the history and physical examination. C
Laparoscopy should be avoided in the initial diagnostic work-up and should be reserved for carefully defined circumstances. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Dysmenorrhea most common feature; also dyspareunia, menstrual dyschezia, subfertility or infertility
Urinary urgency, frequency, and nocturia in the absence of proven urinary tract infection
Dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia, chronic vaginal bleeding, unresponsive to hormonal therapy
Abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pressure, palpable mass on exam
Abnormal physical exam, abnormal radiologic exam, weight loss
Vaginal discharge, history of sexually transmitted infection, or high-risk behavior
Specific palpable trigger points on exam
Multiparous, pelvic heaviness or fullness reported, pelvic varices may be seen, Doppler ultrasound to identify dilated veins
Often loosely defined and poorly studied

list.listitem: Given the broad diagnostic possibilities for CPP, a thorough history including bowel symptoms, menstrual symptoms, sexually transmitted infection history, abuse history, and pain description in addition to a detailed physical examination should be used to guide diagnostic testing. The International Pelvic Pain Society evaluation forms may be helpful for guiding diagnosis and for documentation.

In a small case-control study of 16 women with CPP and 15 age-matched healthy controls, most women with CPP reported dyspareunia, pain with walking, lifting and defecation, as well as pain with a full bladder compared to the few control women reporting these symptoms. Moderately severe generalized autonomic symptomatology was also identified in women with CPP vs. controls, including higher rates of vasomotor and orthostatic symptoms and gastroparesis.

Signs and symptoms observed in women with suspected pelvic congestion syndrome include pain worsened by prolonged standing, coitus, menstruation, and pregnancy, and exam findings of pelvic and/or vulvar varicosities.
Many of the diagnostic possibilities are accompanied by a normal or near-normal physical examination.

In a systematic review, symptoms that most increased the likelihood of ovarian cancer, when present, were abdominal mass (positive likelihood ratio [LR+] 30.0); abdominal distension or increased girth (LR+ 16.0); abdominal or pelvic pain (LR+ 10.4) or bloating (LR+ 9.3); loss of appetite (LR+ 9.2); and family history of ovarian cancer (LR+ 7.5). However, no symptom or combination of symptoms is useful as a screening tool in a low-prevalence population.

NIH-NIDDK criteria for the diagnosis of interstitial cystitis were formed for research purposes and may miss 60% of patients with the disease. A clinical diagnosis on the basis of symptoms of frequency, urgency, nocturia, and pelvic pain in the absence of an infectious process may be more appropriate.

The cotton-tip applicator test, in which gentle pressure is applied to the skin, appears to be a reliable test for identifying cutaneous pain in dermatomes T1–L1 in women and men with CPP. Using this test, 16 of 22 patients with CPP had a positive test compared with no patients in the no pain group and 1 of 12 patients with cyclic pain. This likely occurs because visceral pain can be referred to dermatomes that correspond to the somatic nerve fibers involved in pelvic pain.
Consider transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) in patients with a suspected gynecologic cause who have an inadequate physical examination or a palpable mass.

MRI and TVUS are useful studies for diagnosis of adenomyosis. In a retrospective study of 291 women with CPP, however, MRI had high specificity but low sensitivity for observing deep-infiltrating endometriosis, endometrioma, adhesions, and ovarian cysts using a reference standard of laparoscopy and expert panel diagnosis. The authors concluded that use of MRI did not add value to the history, examination, and ultrasound findings and its use would lead to 369/1000 women with CPP receiving unnecessary laparoscopy and 136/1000 women with CPP who required laparoscopy not receiving it.

See chapter on endometriosis for information on diagnosis using TVUS, rectal US, and MRI. In cases where endometriosis is suspected and there are no other indications for surgery, laparoscopic confirmation of the diagnosis is not necessary. Unnecessary laparoscopy may "medicalize" the problem and create unrealistic expectations regarding cure. It is generally a second-line intervention when empiric treatment for suspected causes has failed, when fertility is a concern because of adhesions or endometriosis, or when a specific intervention is planned. ACOG, however, recommends direct visualization of ectopic endometrial lesions accompanied by histologic confirmation.
See chapter on interstitial cystitis for detailed information on diagnosis of that condition.
The diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome may be made on history and physical examination alone.
Patients with nonspecific abdominal symptoms do not have a higher risk for serious colonic pathology on colonoscopy.

CT-guided pudendal nerve blocks may be valuable diagnostically for patients with suspected pudendal neuralgia, based on a case series, and may be useful in identifying those whose pain will improve with surgical nerve release.
See for a suggested approach to management.
A pregnancy test should be obtained if the woman is of reproductive age.
Completion of a 3-month pain diary may be helpful.

Specific symptoms and/or abnormalities on physical examination (e.g., signs of infection such as fever, gastrointestinal symptoms such as hematochezia) are used to direct further diagnostic and treatment strategies.
Many of the conditions associated with CPP have poorly defined diagnostic criteria.

For gynecologic procedures that can be painful in nature, such as coloposcopy, LEEP, pessary removal and insertion, considerations such as topical lidocaine can be especially helpful for patients with underlying CPP for pain control to best tolerate the procedure.
If a specific diagnosis is made, treat the underlying condition.
Set expectations early. CPP is a chronic disease that will require trial and error with treatment and there is no one-size-fits-all approach.
Use a multidisciplinary approach (medical, surgical, physiotherapy, and psychotherapy). B
First-line medications for pain include acetaminophen, acetylsalicylic acid, and NSAIDs. B

Second-line medications (if pain has a cyclic component) include oral contraceptive pills or combined hormonal vaginal ring, B continuous progestins, B and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) analogues. A

Third-line medications include tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), especially in patients with underlying depression, and opioids. B
If neuropathic pain is suspected TCAs, SNRIs or anticonvulsants can be considered. B
Midline pain associated with menses may be treated with presacral neurectomy. B
Refractory pain can be managed with hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. B
There are few randomized trials on treatment of CPP.
Treatment of CPP can focus on treating the pain, treating the underlying cause, or both.
Treating pain can consist of non-opioid analgesics including acetaminophen, acetylsalicylic acid, and NSAIDs, which are considered first-line therapy for pain relief.

Hormone treatment can be used for pain that has a cyclic component and includes oral contraceptive pills, continuous progestins, or GnRH agonists. The use of long acting progestins or combined oral contraception pills show similar efficacy for pain control.

For refractory pain, options include TCAs, SNRIs, and opioids. In an open 6-month RCT of 150 men with chronic prostatitis/CPP of whom 126 completed the study, the combination of 60 mg duloxetine, an SNRI, and 4 mg doxazosin, an alpha blocker, appeared to be more effective than doxazosin alone or sertraline plus doxazosin for pain reduction and symptom improvement.
For neuropathic pain, options include TCAs, SNRIs, and anticonvulsants (e.g., gabapentin, pregabalin).

In a small pilot RCT of 47 women with CPP, women randomized to gabapentin had less pain and improved mood compared to women on placebo at 6 months. However, in a larger UK RCT of 306 women, aged 18 to 50 years, who had CPP with no obvious pathology on laparoscopy, gabapentin was no more effective than placebo in providing pain relief at 4 months and caused significantly more adverse effects including dizziness (54% vs. 28%) and drowsiness (52% vs. 29%). Average pain and worst pain scores declined in both groups.

In a Cochrane analysis of treatments for CPP, including women with pelvic vein insufficiency and pelvic congestion syndrome, medroxyprogesterone 50 mg once daily, goserelin (a GnRH agonist that provides benefit of longer duration), counseling after a reassuring ultrasound, and a multidisciplinary approach were found to be of definite benefit; adhesiolysis (apart from cases with severe adhesions), uterine nerve ablation, sertraline and photographic reinforcement after laparoscopy were not beneficial. Writing therapy and static magnetic field therapy may offer short-term benefit.

Authors of a Cochrane review found only one small trial on use of an anti-tumor necrosis factor drug (infliximab) for painful endometriosis; no benefit on pain was found. Treatment with danazol, however, was effective in reducing pain and improving laparoscopic scores in these patients; use was limited by androgenic side effects.

In an RCT of 67 women with adenomyosis, dienogest (a synthetic oral progestin, available as Natazia in the United States) significantly reduced adenomyosis-associated back pain compared to placebo at 16 weeks. The main side effect was irregular vaginal bleeding in the dienogest group.
Botulinum toxin injections to the pelvic floor in conjunction with pelvic floor muscle theray have not shown evidence of benefit for chronic pelvic pain management.
Laparoscopic treatment of visible endometriosis leads to improvement in pain and thus supports the recommendation to treat endometriotic lesions seen at the time of diagnostic laparoscopy.

A 2025 systematic review identified factors associated with persistent pain after hysterectomy for CPP. 12-68% of patients had persistent pain. Ovarian conservation and endometriosis severity were not consistently found to be associated with persistent pain, while younger age at surgery was.

Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) is a technique designed to disrupt the efferent nerve fibers in the uterosacral ligament to decrease uterine pain for women with intractable dysmenorrhea. LUNA does not appear to offer any added benefits beyond those that can be achieved with conservative surgery alone.

Presacral neurectomy involves interrupting the sympathetic innervation to the uterus at the level of the superior hypogastric plexus. This procedure has been proposed for treatment of midline pain associated with menses and with endometriosis.
Laparoscopic ovarian vein ligation has been proposed for pelvic vein insufficiency, but supporting data are limited.
Transcatheter pelvic vein embolization may be useful and is supported by case series data for pain reduction.
Not suturing the endometrium can reduce the risk of intermenstrual bleeding and uterine scar defect after cesarean delivery which can be a cause of ongoing pelvic pain.
Levator ani trigger-point injections can be considered for CPP; targeted injections, along with pelvic floor exercise, were shown to be helpful in a small case series.

Acupuncture has been shown in case reports to improve pelvic pain related to endometriosis and might be useful in women with CCP.Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs assessed effect of acupuncture for chronic prostatitis/CPP in men and found that acupuncture was superior to sham acupuncture in improving symptoms.

Herbs proposed as being effective for pelvic pain include black cohosh, chastetree, dong quai, black haw (Viburnum prunifolium), and crampbark (Viburnum poulus); there is a lack of supporting evidence.

There have been some RCTs showing the effectiveness of dietary supplements including thiamine (vitamin B1) at 100 mg per day for 3 months and vitamin E (150-500 IU/day) administered a few days before and during menses.

There is some evidence that a diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids (or supplemental fish oil; 1080 mg icosapentaenoic acid, 720 mg docosahexanoic acid, 1.5 mg vitamin E) can decrease painful menses.In contrast, omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin D supplementation was no better than placebo at decreasing pelvic pain associated with endometriosis.
There is low-quality evidence that chlorella supplementation can reduce PGE2 and PGF2a leading to decreased uterine tone and pelvic pain.

Some studies suggest that leuprolide in combination with combined OCP, elagolix, vitamins C and E, and gestrinone may represent the most effective therapeutic options for alleviating endometriosis-associated pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and nonmenstrual pelvic pain.
Laser therapy has not been shown to be effective for CPP.
A multidisciplinary approach was effective for reducing pain and included physiotherapy, psychotherapy, and attention to dietary and environmental factors.
Mindfulness meditation may be useful, but data are limited.

In a study of women with CPP and comorbid depression, interpersonal psychotherapy was helpful for reducing depression severity and improving social adjustment, but pain interference remained unchanged.
In women with interstitial cystitis, manual physical therapy techniques can be helpful and are recommended by the American Urological Association.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of biopsychosocial therapies for CPP found evidence of benefit for cognitive behavioral therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, and mindfulness. Outcomes studied included vestibulodynia, sexual function, pain level, and quality of life.

Many treatments have been tried for interstitial cystitis (IC); none has been curative. Non-medical treatments such as dietary modifications (avoiding aggravating factors such as caffeine, alcohol, spicy or acidic foods, or artificial sweeteners) and stress management might be helpful. The only oral medication approved for IC is sodium pentosan polysulfate, which can take up to 6 months to be effective.
Treatment of IBS usually starts with stress management and dietary modifications.

For CPP associated with endometriosis, both etonogestrel-releasing implants and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine devices had an equivalent mean reduction in noncyclic pelvic pain by more than half in an unmasked randomized noninferiority trial including 103 women.

The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology currently recommends pelvic floor physical therapy, sex therapy, or cognitive behavioral therapy for complimentary treatment of pelvic pain. These interventions are most effective for pain associated with myofascial and psychosocial etiologies.
In an observational study of patients in a pelvic pain specialty clinic, 46% reported pain reduction and 32% improvement in depression at 1 year. B
The prognosis of CPP varies with the underlying cause. C
Early in the evaluation, discuss with patients that the overall goal may be symptom reduction and that a diagnosis might not be made. C

About 45% of all pregnant women and 25% of all postpartum women suffer from pelvic girdle pain and/or low back pain. In a study based on data from the Danish National Birth Cohort, 18.5% of all pregnant women reported pregnancy-related pelvic pain.

The pelvic girdle questionnaire consisting of 20 activity items and 5 symptom items has been developed for use in assessing and monitoring patients with pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy and post-partum; it appears to have acceptably high reliability and validity.

In a systematic review, motion of the pelvic girdle joints is 32% to 68% greater in patients with pelvic or low back pain than in healthy controls, suggesting that excessive motion plays a role in pain.

Risk factors for pelvic pain among pregnant women include overweight and obesity (adjusted OR 1.2 [95% CI, 1.1-1.4] in overweight women, 1.5 [95% CI, 1.2-2.0] in obese women Class 1 (30≤BMI<35), and 1.9 [95% CI, 1.3-2.8] in obese women Class 2 + 3 (BMI ≥35)), increasing parity (1 previous delivery OR 1.9 [95% CI, 1.9-2.0] and 2 previous deliveries OR 2.4 [95% CI, 2.3-2.6]), and possibly smoking (adjusted odds ratio of 1.2 (95% CI, 1.0-1.4).

Cochrane authors found low-quality evidence and no benefit from group exercise when added to information about managing pain and usual prenatal care in the number of women reporting pelvic pain. However, there is low quality evidence that an exercise program may reduce pregnancy-related low-back and pelvic pain and moderate- to low-quality evidence suggesting that exercise improves functional disability and reduces sick leave more than usual care.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies of pregnant women found support for manual therapy on pain intensity when compared to usual care and relaxation, but not when compared to sham interventions.

There is moderate evidence from 4 trials that exercise, acupuncture and pelvic supports improve functional outcomes in pregnant women with low back or pelvic pain. Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs of acupuncture for chronic prostatitis/CPP found acupuncture to be superior to sham acupuncture in improving symptoms.

Craniosacral therapy may reduce morning pain and improve function in pregnant women with pelvic girdle pain, but did not alter evening pain or rates of sick leave. The differences seen may not be clinically significant.

cell.label: Pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis persisting for at least 6 months and severe enough to cause functional disability
• Consider urinalysis and culture as well as screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea. • Treat infection.

• Work up any specific abnormalities on physical examination and treat any infections. • Address any psychosocial factors and discuss possibility of symptom improvement without diagnosis, as well as possible need for multidisciplinary approach.

• Screen for alarm symptoms such as hematochezia, melena, significant weight loss, or pain severe enough to awaken from sleep. • Consider fecal occult blood testing. • Trial of diet and bowel program.
• Reevaluate. • Consider stool studies, endoscopy, referral.
Symptoms are suggestive of a gynecologic cause?
• Diagnosis unclear: early multidisciplinary approach is appropriate.
• Check urinalysis, consider culture. • Urinalysis negative symptoms suggest interstitial cystitis, conservative treatment or referral. • Hematuria without obvious infection, consider referral.
• Consider transvaginal ultrasound. • Consider trial of hormonal treatment, including combined oral contraceptive pills or a GnRH agonist for 3-6 months.
• Continue hormonal treatment. • Consider addition of NSAIDs.
